scenes.narration: One condition is often not enough. Today we combine them, and meet the strange idea that a value can be false without being the word False.

scenes.onScreen: "Combining conditions": three numbered lines (1. and needs both sides True; 2. or needs at least one side True; 3. not flips True and False) and an analogy card: a beach club entry: you need a ticket AND to be eighteen; a child OR a senior walks in free
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Three small words combine conditions. And is True only when both sides are True. Or is True when at least one side is True. Not flips the answer. Think of a beach club. To enter, you need a ticket and you need to be eighteen. A child or a senior citizen walks in free. Python also treats some values as false by themselves. Zero, an empty string, and None all count as False.

scenes.onScreen: gate.py: and, or and not on an age and a ticket

scenes.onScreen: A small truth table for and, or and not with rows for True and False, and a list of values that count as False: 0, empty string, None

scenes.narration: Here is the truth table. And is True only in one row, when both are True. Or is False only in one row, when both are False. Not simply flips. Python also has a short list of values that count as False by themselves. Zero, an empty string, an empty list, and None. Almost everything else counts as True.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: x equals one or two
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. Choice is three. We want to know if it is one or two. The program says Valid. Wrong! Python reads this as, choice equals one, or two. And the plain number two is always true. So the whole condition is always true. Write the comparison in full on both sides, choice equals one, or choice equals two, and it works.

props.why: Python reads the wrong line as (choice == 1) or 2, and the number 2 is always truthy, so the whole condition is always True.

shorts.title: And, or, not
shorts.script: Three small words combine conditions. And is True only when both sides are True. Or is True when at least one side is True. Not flips the answer, so True becomes False. Think of a beach club. You need a ticket and an adult age to enter. A child or a senior citizen enters free. Combine conditions, and you can describe almost any rule. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Combine conditions.

shorts.title: Truth table
shorts.hook: "Here is the whole truth table in one go."
shorts.script: Here is the whole truth table in one go. And is True in just one case, when both sides are True. Or is False in just one case, when both sides are False. Not flips whatever it gets. That is all there is to it. If you ever feel lost with a long condition, draw this table on paper, and test each part. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: The whole table.

shorts.title: Truthy and falsy
shorts.hook: "Some values count as False without being the word False."
shorts.script: Some values count as False without being the word False. Zero is False. An empty string is False. An empty list is False. And so is None. Almost everything else counts as True. So if name, with no comparison, means, is the name not empty? It is a very short, very Pythonic way to check that something has a value. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Falsy values.

shorts.title: One or two
shorts.script: Here is a famous trap. You write if choice equals one or two. Python reads that as, choice equals one, or the plain number two. And the number two is always truthy. So the condition is always True, even when choice is three. Write the comparison in full on both sides of the or, and the trap disappears. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Write both comparisons.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.script: Why was the boolean so calm? It knew when to say and, and when to say or. Your challenge. Make age equal four. Print Free if age is below five, or above sixty. Otherwise print Pay. Then test the ages five, sixty, and sixty one. Do the edges give the answers you expect? Tell us in the comments. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 15.
